A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on four domain-adaptation benchmarks, synthetic experiments, weighting-error analyses and repeated-run results.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds spectral analyses, SSL component ablations and further method comparisons.

M1.justification: v2 introduces evaluated alignment-plus-uniformity and Barlow Twins alternatives to the existing target-SSL module (Section 4.1 and Appendix B.3). The core approach of adding target SSL to domain adaptation remains, and Appendix D.4 still specifies the same default SimSiam implementation.

E1.justification: The four benchmark datasets, domains and tabulated general/extreme class counts are retained. v2 Figure 9 extends the overlap-spectrum evaluation to open-set and partial-adaptation boundary scenarios where one domain has no private classes, beyond v1's principal SPCR sweep.

E2.justification: v2 adds MLNet and MLNet+SSL to the extreme-setting comparisons across all four benchmarks (Tables 3–4), while retaining UAN, CMU, DANCE and UniOT. Appendix B.3 additionally compares AlignUniform and Barlow Twins against SimSiam. DANCE's regrouping under self-training is not a newly added baseline.

E3.justification: New spectral controls vary labeled-target availability across 10%, 50% and 100%. The rotation-based, multiclass toy experiment is replaced by a three-class construction varying source-private sample counts between 50 and 2500. Figure 4 also changes the reported outcome from target-common-to-source-private misclassification to shared-class accuracy; this does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds singular-value analyses of source-private dominance and labeled-target controls, separates alignment and uniformity through ablations, and compares three SSL frameworks. Its redesigned toy experiments examine collapse and clustering separately. The target-private SSL and hyperparameter-sensitivity studies are retained as Figures 10–11 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix A.2/Table 6 and v2 Appendix B.4/Table 8 report the same three different-seed runs and identical means and standard deviations for six Office31 transfers. No additional uncertainty-reporting procedure or increased run count is documented.

E6.justification: Shared benchmark rows retain their numerical values, but substantial results are added for MLNet, SSL alternatives, component ablations and spectral analyses. For example, v2 Table 3 adds DomainNet averages of 47.8/48.9 for MLNet without/with SSL; Table 2 reports 64.5, 64.6, 65.1 and 67.2 for source-only, alignment, uniformity and both components. These are additional comparisons, not improvements to unchanged v1 result entries.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the principal SPCR definition with normalized source-private and target-private proportions over the union of label sets, and explicitly formulates uniformity loss. The weighting-error formula is retained under the name EIW. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on source-private feature bias and an SSL debiasing module. v2 identifies dimensional collapse as the primary cause, makes uniformity central to its remedy, and claims state-of-the-art performance toward comprehensive UniDA in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 develops a specific collapse-to-weighting-error mechanism, distinguishes alignment's clustering benefit from its potential to worsen collapse, and attributes dimensional preservation to uniformity. It also newly explains larger adversarial-training gains through greater sensitivity to weighting errors. The qualification that target-private SSL can hurt performance is retained.

D1.justification: v2 discloses alphabetical class partitioning, the covariance/SVD analysis procedure, and explicit toy distributions, sample counts and network output sizes. The principal backbone, training budget, batch size and SimSiam settings remain unchanged. v1's explicit instruction to flip binary alignment weights is reduced to a less specific controlled-error description.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around dimensional-collapse research and modern contrastive/non-contrastive SSL, adding a dedicated collapse review and an SSL comparison table. New references include Jing et al., Wang and Isola, and Zbontar et al. Its discussion also expands to source-free and generalized UniDA and revises the taxonomy of domain-matching methods.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and central explanatory narrative are extensively rewritten. Background and limitations become separate sections, terminology changes to partial domain matching, and related work, implementation details and several analyses are reorganized into expanded appendices.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. v2 adds spectrum and singular-value plots, replaces the toy visualizations, and replaces the one-dimensional robustness display with contour plots. Tables gain importance-weight columns and revised grouping; retained figures and tables are also split or relocated.

improvement.justification: The spectral controls, SSL component ablations and MLNet comparisons strengthen the explanation and empirical assessment beyond v1's evidence. However, the revised toy experiment varies sample imbalance as a proxy for class-count ratios, and Appendix D.5 specifies an invalid covariance matrix with determinant -20, limiting reproducibility. These weaknesses temper the gains and support a limited overall improvement.
